header:
Date: 2025-02-14
Time: 16:00 - 16:52 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Platform: Zoom (recording available)
Attendees: Sarah Miller (Redwood AE), Tom Nguyen (Redwood SE), Lina Ortiz (SolicoRe Head of Platform), Raj Patel (Staff ML Eng), Marta Silva (Security Lead), Ethan Cole (Infra Lead)
summary: Demo focused on handling long conversational contexts with sustained high TPS, streaming backpressure behavior and timeout strategies. Walked through Redwood Console Optimize suggestions, KV cache behavior, routing to Dedicated vs Hosted, and Private VPC considerations. Agreed next steps for a 48-hour benchmark and sharing security docs.
topics: Dedicated vs Hosted vs Private deployment tradeoffs
security: SSO, KMS, audit logs, SOC2
transcript:
00:00 Sarah (AE): hi everyone thanks for carving this out especially on valentine's day, appreciate it. we wanted to show a focused demo around the edge conditions you mentioned in the questionnaire — long sessions, sustained TPS and what happens when streaming queues start to build up.
00:14 Lina: thanks Sarah yeah excited. we've seen sporadic tail latency spikes when session history grows, and some clients time out and retry which creates surge loops.
00:29 Tom (SE): great, i'll share my screen now. quick note: we'll demo via Hosted first then flip to Dedicated config and show console optimize suggestions. if you see any numbers that don't line up that's probably live infra wobble, please call it out.
00:47 Raj: one ask upfront — our production has mixed chat+retrieval pipelines, so context sizes vary a lot; we want to see behavior at 150k token active context, and at 250k in a stress step.
01:05 Tom (SE): ok we'll start with 150k. i'm going to simulate 1200 rps steady state with a mix of streaming and non-streaming calls, prefix cache warmed. note — our KV cache is per session and is LRU by default, eviction policy configurable. sometimes docs call it K V cash in transcripts, but it's the KV cache.
01:28 Sarah (AE): also quick callouts for the team: security will want SSO, audit logs, KMS integration; infra will want predictable latency and predictable failure modes.
01:40 Marta: yes, SOC2 is table stakes. we need to know what audit logs look like and how keys are rotated in Private deployments.
01:52 Tom (SE): show console — here is Optimize tab. it analyzes your token distribution and recommends batching window, kv cache size and quantization candidate models. for long contexts it will surface when prefix caching gives diminishing returns and recommend partial truncation or compressed summaries.
02:15 Ethan: can Optimize suggest a fallback model when primary model is fully saturated? like route to a cheaper quantized variant?
02:24 Tom (SE): yes, that's the routing policy rule you can set — latency-first or cost-first. we can set automatic fallback to a quantized variant on capacity strain, and that shows up in the console rollout policy where you can do canary % and automatic fallback thresholds.
02:41 Raj: show me the streaming backpressure behavior — what does the client see when the server is overloaded and tokens are buffering? we've had clients hold open connections for minutes.
02:53 Tom (SE): demoing streaming now. pretend client opens stream and we throttle per-connection to avoid head-of-line blocking. you'll see a server side token backlog metric. if backlog exceeds threshold we emit a backpressure event and do one of three things, configurable: 1) shed older sessions, 2) fallback to non-streaming buffered response (full response delivered when ready), 3) degrade model to smaller context or quantized model.
03:23 Lina: when you say shed older sessions what does that mean practically? we can't lose user state.
03:29 Tom (SE): shedding in our terms is graceful: we prioritize active sessions, then for low-priority idle sessions we persist the KV cache snapshot to cold store and terminate the live inference; clients get a specific 429-like code with retry-after and a reason header so SDK knows to back off or to rehydrate.
03:51 Raj: ok and what about partial response semantics? some of our UIs rely on partial tokens arriving to render streaming progressively.
03:59 Tom (SE): we support partial streaming with chunked frames; if we switch to buffered mode we still return a partial prefix if available, otherwise client will see a stall then a final payload. SDKs expose a streaming mode flag and backoff handlers. i should call out that client-side timeouts need to be tuned: we've seen customers set 5s timeouts and then when a backlog hits they retry causing thundering herd.
04:23 Marta: so best practice is longer client timeouts plus exponential backoff?
04:27 Tom (SE): yes, and prefer idempotent retry tokens. also set the SDK to honor the retry-after header emitted by Redwood.
04:35 Sarah (AE): question from me — customers often wonder if Dedicated avoids all of this. what's the right way to frame Dedicated vs Hosted for their case?
04:42 Tom (SE): Dedicated gives you capacity isolation so noisy neighbors are gone, but you still have to design for long context memory pressure — the kernel selection and KV cache sizing matter. Dedicated reduces inter-tenant variability, but doesn't remove the need for streaming guardrails.
05:01 Raj: curious about memory usage for 250k tokens — is that linear? we've had cases where session memory spikes nonlinearly due to attention cache.
05:10 Tom (SE): good point — attention KV is roughly linear with sequence length but operationally other recopies (like activations for long prefix compression) can spike. we instrument per-session kv_memory_bytes and have thresholds in Console to auto-evict or compress older history. Optimize will recommend a compression cadence (e.g., summarize every 10k tokens) with tradeoff curves.
05:34 Ethan: show the trace view in Console for a slowed session.
05:37 Tom (SE): switching to trace tab. here you see per-token latency, queue depth, kernel selected and model variant. note the trace has a fuzzy transcription of model names sometimes in older logs (eg 'red wood big small' instead of proper model id) — we cleaned up new logs but older ones may be noisy.
06:00 Lina: on failover — if primary region goes down what happens to in-flight streaming sessions?
06:06 Tom (SE): in-flight sessions can't be migrated mid-token; we do a graceful fallback: complete tokens on primary, then if region fails we route new requests to fallback region and allow clients to rehydrate session from persisted KV snapshot — there will be a last-token gap. for strict RPO you'd want geo-redundant replication and that is part of Redwood Dedicated enterprise add-on.
06:33 Raj: great. toggling to long-run benchmark — Tom can you explain how you'll simulate the 48h run?
06:39 Tom (SE): plan: run a synthetic generator with a mix of session lengths: 60% short (<2k tokens), 30% medium (10k-50k), 10% heavy (>150k), sustained RPS ramp from 500 to 1800, periodic spikes, and some clients streaming. we'll record per-minute histograms for p50/p95/p99, backlog events, and session eviction counts. we'll attach the raw traces.
07:02 Sarah (AE): quick security note — Marta, infrastructure paperwork: are you ok with Redwood's SOC2 Type II and crosswalk or do you want syslog/SIEM forwarding?
07:13 Marta: SOC2 is fine but we need syslog forward and KMS key control in our VPC for private deployments. what about HSM?
07:20 Tom (SE): KMS integration is supported; for on-prem or Private we can plug customer-managed HSM for keys. syslog/SIEM forwarding is available via event streams. we'll send the security integration doc after the call.
07:34 Lina: any hard limits we should be aware of? like maximum context length enforced by runtime or token budget?
07:40 Tom (SE): runtime supports up to ~500k tokens in a session but performance degrades; we recommend testing at your profile. beyond a threshold we suggest compressed summaries rather than full retention. also watch per-VM memory caps on Dedicated nodes.
08:01 Raj: show me how batching affects latency at high TPS — does batching introduce tail spikes?
08:07 Tom (SE): batching improves throughput but can increase latency if your batching window is too long. Optimize recommends an adaptive batching window based on arrival jitter; for high TPS with low jitter batching window can be 8-12ms and not impact p95 much. in low TPS bursts we fall back to immediate single-request paths.
08:32 Ethan: what about token billing when we compress or summarize history? do you bill on stored compressed tokens or original tokens?
08:38 Sarah (AE): billing granularity: generation tokens and input tokens. compression/summary reduces future input tokens and thus reduces billable units over time. we'll share a primer on how compression affects unit economics.
08:52 Raj: any changes to model quality when we quantize or fallback? we have tight quality SLAs for top-tier users.
08:58 Tom (SE): yes there's a tradeoff. quantized models can have slight drop in generation quality; Optimize will run golden prompt evals and provide a quality delta. we can gate rollouts on eval thresholds — e.g., only fallback if quality delta < 2% on your evaluation set.
09:22 Marta: do you keep request payloads in logs? we need redaction guarantees.
09:27 Tom (SE): PII redaction is configurable. by default we store metadata and token counts, not full prompts. if you need full prompts we can enable them but they'll be encrypted and access-controlled. for Private deployments you can disable prompt retention entirely.
09:44 Lina: let's talk about SDK behavior again — if a client has a 30s timeout but server is buffering for 40s what happens?
09:51 Tom (SE): if the client times out, they'll see a socket close and should honor idempotency token to retry. we emit a final event to storage so client can rehydrate later. again the SDK has helpers to surface retry-after and to do exponential backoff.
10:09 Raj: curious about how you surface per-route cost in Console. can we map cost to feature flags?
10:15 Tom (SE): yes, Console has per-route cost attribution and you can tag routes; Optimize will then recommend quantization per route or cache TTLs per tag. this lets product teams toggle expensive features per user segment.
10:29 Ethan: any gotchas with Private VPC networking? we've had trouble with NAT timeouts when long-lived client streams exist through load balancers.
10:35 Tom (SE): recommended pattern is direct peering or private link for long-lived streams. ALB/NLB with long idle timeouts can drop streams; we recommend TCP-level keepalives and adjust LB idle timeouts or prefer a proxy that supports long-lived websockets. we'll include network checklist.
10:56 Sarah (AE): quick pricing framing: Dedicated reduces per-token variance but has a monthly commit. we'll share examples for 3-month pilot vs 12-month commit.
11:08 Lina: what's the minimum pilot we can run to validate? we want to reproduce our hot path — say 6-hour window at 1k RPS with 50% heavy sessions?
11:16 Tom (SE): you can do a targeted 48h pilot but we can scope a 6-12 hour smoke test first and then expand. for billing we can do a short-term burst allotment on Dedicated trial.
11:29 Raj: show me the console alerting for queue/backpressure.
11:33 Tom (SE): alerting is based on metrics: queue_depth, session_eviction_rate, backlog_events. thresholds can trigger runbooks in Console and integrate with PagerDuty. we also have automatic pre-populated runbooks for common backpressure patterns.
11:51 Marta: if we need compliance review can we get network diagrams and deployment hardening checklist?
11:57 Sarah (AE): yes we'll include that in the security packet.
12:05 Lina: any live example of a cascading retry-induced outage and how Redwood mitigated it?
12:10 Tom (SE): we had a retail customer where client SDKs retried aggressively and caused a waveform surge. Redwood mitigated by enabling rate-limited edge proxies, adding a retry-after on overloaded endpoints and switching non-critical sessions to buffered responses. console telemetry showed backlog spikes and then auto-fallback engaged.
12:35 Ethan: curious about how Redis or cut-to-cold store interacts with KV snapshotting. is that pluggable?
12:41 Tom (SE): yes you can plug your own object store for snapshots, and snapshot frequency/TTL is configurable per deployment. for Dedicated we usually use a managed blob store with lifecycle rules.
12:56 Raj: ok this is helpful. can you also include a small runbook for client SDK tuning?
13:01 Tom (SE): yes will attach SDK tuning doc — recommended timeouts, idempotency tokens, retry-after handling, and streaming/window sizes.
13:12 Sarah (AE): we should recap next steps. Tom you'll run the 48-hour bench and attach traces, Sarah will send pricing and security docs, customer will share traces. anyone else?
13:22 Lina: thanks yes Marta will compile compliance questions.
13:26 Marta: and i'll need an SLA appendix for Dedicated.
13:30 Sarah (AE): great, last thing — do you want a follow-up deep-dive with infra-only team?
13:36 Lina: yes please week of 2/24.
13:40 Sarah (AE): perfect. thanks everyone. we'll follow up in email with links to the demo spreadsheet and the security packet. bye.
13:46 (call ends)

Notes on transcript: occasional transcription artifacts present (eg 'K V cash' for KV cache, 'red wood' for Redwood). timestamps approximate; speaker labels largely accurate though Zoom sometimes merged overlapping talk.
